blocks.text: The rite by which the Jews slaughtered turtledoves and doves is taught briefly by Moses in Levit. I, 15. 16. 17. and V, 8., and at greater length by the Talmudists in Zebachim ch. 6, fol. 64, and by Maimonides in the book On the offering of sacrifices ch. 6, §§ 20, 21, 22, 23, and ch. 7, §§ 6, 7, 8. Much could be drawn from these that is not altogether commonplace, if that were our present business. But here it will suffice to have noted that the Hebrews slaughtered other victims with a blade, but birds with the fingernail alone, by which, with the head bent back, their throat was torn open. In Hebrew this is מלק, which the Greeks render ἀποκνίζειν [apoknizein], that is, to tear with the nail, or to cut off, Levit. I, 15. and V, 8., the only places where it occurs. The Jerusalem Targum has עום, and Jonathan חום, which is the same, ח and ע being interchanged. In Arabic the same is حذم [ḥadhama] or خذم [khadhama], which they render to cut and to tear apart. Thus خذمت الصقر [khadhamat al-ṣaqr], the hawk tore with its talons, in Alcamus. Kimchi, in his Lexicon under the word מלק, describes the rite of tearing the bird thus: ואר״זל כיצד מולקין חטאת העוף נותן שתי גפיה בין שתי אצבעותיו ושתי רגליה בין שתי אצבעותיו והיה מותח צוארה על שתי אצבעותיו והיה מולק בצפורן ממול עורף עד שמגיע לסימנים וקוצץ אותן או רובן ואינו מבדיל שנאמר ולא יבדיל אבל בעולה העוף שאמר ומלק את ראשו ולא אמר ולא יבדיל הוא מולק ומבדיל הראש בעצמו הגוף בעצמו Our masters of blessed memory said: How was the sin offering of a bird torn? He (the priest) placed its wings between two fingers and its feet between two fingers, and stretched its neck over his two fingers, and cut with his nail opposite the nape until he reached the signs (in the throat), which he severed, or the greater part of them, yet so that he did not divide it, because it is said Levit. V, 8. „And he shall not divide it“. But in the burnt offering of a bird, because it is said, „He shall wring off its head“, and it is not added, „And he shall not divide it“, Levit. I, 15., he cut so that the head was separated from the trunk of the body. So he, from the passage of the Talmud we have cited. See also Maimonides, who asserts that this was מעבודות קשות שבמקדש, one of the most laborious services of the Sanctuary, in the book On the offering of sacrifices ch. 7, § 8 ^{(1)}.

[II, 559] So that victims should not be lacking, in the first part of the temple, which was called פרבר parbar, 1 Paral. XXVI, 18., oxen, sheep and doves were sold, Ioh. II, 14. Accordingly in Maimonides' treatise On the vessels of the Sanctuary ch. 7, § 9 (among the officers of the temple, whom the Hebrews called ממוני המקדש and the Greeks στρατηγοὺς τοῦ ἱεροῦ [stratēgous tou hierou], Luc. XXII, 52.) there is listed הממונה שעל הקינים, the officer over the nests, that is, over the birds. And he is described thus: הדא שפוסקין עמו שימכור הקנים לקורבנות כך וכך בסלע וכל מי שהוא חייב תורים או שני בני יונה יביא דמיהם למקדשי [col. 27] וזה הממונה נותן הקנים לבעלי הקורבנות ועושה חשבון עם הגוברים ונותנין לו משלושים יום לשלושים יום, He is the one with whom they contract that he provide birds for the offerings, so many or so many for a shekel. And whoever was obliged to offer either turtledoves or young doves brought the price to the sanctuary. And this officer gave the birds to those whose duty it was to offer, and valued them with the treasurers; and, once he had agreed on the price, they paid him within three days. And a little later: וכן קן שנמצא פסול או שנפסל קודם שיקרוב נותן אחר תחתיו, And if any bird was found unfit, or became unfit (through ceremonial defilement) before it was offered, he gave another in its place. That these arrangements were devised for gain by greedy and avaricious priests, Jerome teaches in these words on Matthew ch. 21: According to the commandments of the Law, in the temple of the Lord, the most confined in the whole world, with the people flocking there from almost all the regions of the Jews, innumerable victims were sacrificed, especially on feast days: bulls, rams and he-goats, while the poor, so as not to be without a sacrifice, offered young doves and turtledoves. It often happened that those who had come from afar had no victims. The priests therefore devised a way to make a prey of the people: they sold all the animals needed for the sacrifices, so that they might both sell to those who had none and themselves receive back again what had been bought. Hence Christ, rightly and justly angered against these profiteers, overturned the seats of those who sold doves, Matth. XXI, 12. and Marc. XI, 15. And to those who sold doves he said, Take these things hence. Do not make my father's house a house of trade, Ioh. II, 16.
